title: Αἰετὸς καὶ νεβρός
titleEn: The Eagle and the Fawn — Iliad 8.198–291
about: Hector’s boast stirs Hera, who urges Poseidon to join her in holding Zeus off from the Trojans; Poseidon refuses to fight against Zeus. On the plain Hector presses the Achaeans back and would have burned the ships, but Hera puts it in Agamemnon’s mind to rouse the army. He stands at Odysseus’ ship, in the middle of the line, and shames the Argives for the boasts they made at Lemnos, then prays to Zeus that the army at least escape. Zeus pities him and sends an eagle that drops a fawn beside his altar. The Achaeans take heart: Diomedes is the first to drive out across the ditch, and kills Agelaus; the other leaders follow. Teucer shoots Trojan after Trojan from under the shield of his half-brother Ajax, and Agamemnon, glad to see it, promises him a prize if the city falls.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, νεμέσησε δὲ πότνια Ἥρη,
σείσατο δ’ εἰνὶ θρόνῳ, ἐλέλιξε δὲ μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
καί ῥα Ποσειδάωνα μέγαν θεὸν ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, declaring, and felt resentment, lady Hera,
and she shook herself on her throne, and shook tall Olympus,
and to Poseidon, great god, face to face she spoke:
sentences.i: So he declared aloud, and lady Hera felt resentment; she shook herself on her throne and shook tall Olympus, and spoke to Poseidon, the great god, face to face:
sentences.n: Hera answers the end of Hector’s speech in the previous part. ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος is the stock closing of a speech, with εὐχόμενος in its sense ‘declaring, vaunting’, not ‘praying’; ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο with its last vowel cut off. νεμέσησε is the aorist of νεμεσάω ‘feel righteous resentment’, and πότνια Ἥρη ‘lady Hera’ is its subject. σείσατο is a middle aorist, ‘she shook herself’; εἰνί is epic ἐνί ‘on’, and ἐλέλιξε is the aorist of ἐλελίζω ‘make tremble’, so Olympus quakes when she moves. Ποσειδάωνα is the epic uncontracted accusative of Ποσειδῶν, μέγαν θεόν ‘great god’ is an epithet of his, and ἀντίον ηὔδα means ‘spoke to him face to face’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἐννοσίγαι’ εὐρυσθενές, οὐδέ νυ σοί περ
ὀλλυμένων Δαναῶν ὀλοφύρεται ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός.
sentences.l:
“Ah, earth-shaker, of wide strength, not even to you, now,
for the perishing Danaans does the heart grieve in your wits.
sentences.i: “Ah, earth-shaker of far-reaching strength, not even your own heart grieves within you for the Danaans as they perish.
sentences.n: Hera begins with the same words of address that Zeus used to Poseidon at 7.455. ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise or dismay, ἐννοσίγαι’ is the vocative ἐννοσίγαιε ‘earth-shaker’ with its last vowel cut off, and εὐρυσθενές ‘of wide strength’ is the vocative of εὐρυσθενής. οὐδέ … περ is ‘not even’, with σοί ‘to you’; ὀλλυμένων Δαναῶν is a genitive after ὀλοφύρεται ‘grieves for’, ὀλλυμένων being the present participle of ὄλλυμαι ‘perish’. θυμός ‘heart, spirit’ is the subject, and ἐν φρεσί ‘in your wits’ says where it sits.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ τοι εἰς Ἑλίκην τε καὶ Αἰγὰς δῶρ’ ἀνάγουσι
πολλά τε καὶ χαρίεντα· σὺ δέ σφισι βούλεο νίκην.
sentences.l:
while they, for you, to Helice and Aegae bring up gifts,
many and pleasing; and you, for them, wish victory.
sentences.i: But they bring many pleasing gifts for you up to Helice and Aegae; wish them victory.
sentences.n: οἳ ‘they’ are the Danaans, and τοι is σοι ‘to you’, the one for whom the gifts are meant. Helice and Aegae are named as places of Poseidon’s worship, as the gifts brought there show; ἀνάγουσι is ‘bring up’, and πολλά τε καὶ χαρίεντα is ‘many and pleasing’. σὺ δέ σφισι βούλεο νίκην is ‘and you, wish them victory’: βούλεο is the imperative of βούλομαι with the epic ending -εο (Attic βούλου), and σφισι is the epic dative plural of the pronoun, ‘for them’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ κ’ ἐθέλοιμεν, ὅσοι Δαναοῖσιν ἀρωγοί,
Τρῶας ἀπώσασθαι καὶ ἐρυκέμεν εὐρύοπα Ζῆν,
αὐτοῦ κ’ ἔνθ’ ἀκάχοιτο καθήμενος οἶος ἐν Ἴδῃ.
sentences.l:
For if indeed we should wish, as many as are helpers to the Danaans,
the Trojans to thrust off and to hold back far-thundering Zeus,
right there he would be grieved, sitting alone on Ida.”
sentences.i: If all of us who are the Danaans’ helpers were willing to drive the Trojans away and hold back Zeus who thunders from afar, he would be grieved right there, sitting alone on Ida.”
sentences.n: The sentence is a condition: εἰ with the optative (ἐθέλοιμεν ‘we should be willing’), and κε with the optative in the main clause (ἀκάχοιτο ‘he would be grieved’). ὅσοι Δαναοῖσιν ἀρωγοί is ‘as many as are helpers to the Danaans’, the gods who favour the Danaans. ἀπώσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust off’ and ἐρυκέμεν the infinitive of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’ in epic -μεν (Attic ἐρύκειν); εὐρύοπα Ζῆν is ‘far-thundering Zeus’, Ζῆν being an accusative of Ζεύς (= Δία). αὐτοῦ … ἔνθα is ‘right there, on the spot’, and καθήμενος οἶος ἐν Ἴδῃ is ‘sitting alone on Ida’, where Zeus has sat since 8.51. Hera’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη κρείων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.l: Her, greatly vexed, addressed the lord earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, the lord earth-shaker said to her:
sentences.n: A reply-formula. τήν ‘her’ is Hera; μέγ’ ὀχθήσας is ‘greatly vexed’ (μέγα adverbial, ὀχθήσας the aorist participle of ὀχθέω), and προσέφη is ‘addressed’ (aorist of προσφημί). κρείων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘the lord earth-shaker’, Poseidon; ἐνοσίχθων is built on ἔνοσις ‘shaking’ and χθών ‘earth’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: Ἥρη ἀπτοεπὲς ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Hera, reckless-of-speech, what sort of word is this you have spoken.
sentences.i: “Hera, reckless talker, what kind of word is this that you have spoken.
sentences.n: Poseidon answers Hera. ἀπτοεπές is the vocative of ἀπτοεπής, a rare adjective built on ἔπος ‘word’; its first part is not securely understood, and ‘reckless of speech’ is only the traditional gloss. ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες is ‘what sort of word have you spoken’, a rebuke, with ἔειπες the epic aorist of εἶπον and the Greek ending the sentence with a full stop, not a question mark.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγ’ ἐθέλοιμι Διὶ Κρονίωνι μάχεσθαι
ἡμέας τοὺς ἄλλους, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερός ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
Not I, for my part, would be willing, against Zeus, the son of Cronus, to fight,
we the others, since indeed by far stronger he is.”
sentences.i: I, for one, would not want the rest of us to fight against Zeus, the son of Cronus, since he is by far the stronger.”
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι, ‘I would not be willing’, is the optative with ἄν. The infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ takes Διὶ Κρονίωνι ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’ in the dative, and has its own subject in the accusative, ἡμέας τοὺς ἄλλους ‘the rest of us’ (ἡμέας is the epic form of ἡμᾶς). ἦ ‘truly’ strengthens the reason, and φέρτερος ‘stronger’ is a comparative. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.l: So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking;
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another;
sentences.n: The scene with the gods closes and the narrative turns to the plain. ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα … ἀγόρευον is a stock line that rounds off an exchange: οἳ μέν ‘they, for their part’ are the two gods, and ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ὅσον ἐκ νηῶν ἀπὸ πύργου τάφρος ἔεργε
πλῆθεν ὁμῶς ἵππων τε καὶ ἀνδρῶν ἀσπιστάων
εἰλομένων·
sentences.i: And all the ground that the ditch shut in, out from the ships and the wall, was crowded with their horses and shield-bearing men, pressed together;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ must mean the Achaeans, whom the previous part left in retreat. ὅσον … τάφρος ἔεργε is ‘as much as the ditch shut in’, ἔεργε being the imperfect of ἔργω ‘shut in, enclose’. ἐκ νηῶν ἀπὸ πύργου, ‘out from the ships, away from the wall’ (πύργος is ‘tower’, here the wall), gives the span tersely, and its exact reach is not spelled out. πλῆθεν is the imperfect of πλήθω ‘be full’, with the genitives ἵππων … ἀνδρῶν ἀσπιστάων ‘of horses and of men, shield-bearers’. εἰλομένων is the middle participle of εἴλω ‘press, crowd together’; the same verb returns as an active in the next line.

sentences.t:
εἴλει δὲ θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης, ὅτε οἱ Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκε.
sentences.l:
was pressing them, the equal of swift Ares,
Hector, Priam’s-son, when to him Zeus gave glory.
sentences.i: and Hector, the son of Priam, the equal of swift Ares, was pressing them in, when Zeus gave him glory.
sentences.n: εἴλει is the active imperfect of the verb seen in εἰλομένων, ‘was pressing’; its object, the Achaeans, is not stated. θοῷ ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ is ‘the equal of swift Ares’: ἀτάλαντος, ‘of equal weight’, takes the dative, and θοῷ is ‘swift’. Πριαμίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Priam’. ὅτε οἱ Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκε is ‘when Zeus gave him glory’, κῦδος being the glory that a god grants in battle and οἱ ‘to him’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ἐνέπρησεν πυρὶ κηλέῳ νῆας ἐΐσας,
εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι πότνια Ἥρη
αὐτῷ ποιπνύσαντι θοῶς ὀτρῦναι Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
And now indeed he would have burned with blazing fire the well-balanced ships,
had not into Agamemnon’s mind put it lady Hera,
himself bustling swiftly to urge on the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And then he would have burned the well-balanced ships with blazing fire, had not lady Hera put it into the mind of Agamemnon to bustle about quickly himself and urge on the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Hector is the subject of ἐνέπρησεν, the aorist of ἐμπίμπρημι ‘set on fire’; the sentence is contrary to fact: καί νύ κε … ἐνέπρησεν …, εἰ μὴ … θῆκε is ‘he would have burned …, had not … put’ (the epic κ’ is κε). πυρὶ κηλέῳ is ‘with blazing fire’, κηλέῳ being a traditional epithet of fire whose exact meaning is uncertain, and νῆας ἐΐσας is the stock ‘well-balanced ships’, the sense of ἐΐσας itself being uncertain. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε is ‘put into his mind’; the infinitive ὀτρῦναι ‘to urge on’ says what Hera put there, and αὐτῷ ποιπνύσαντι ‘for him himself to bustle about’ (the aorist participle of ποιπνύω) is in the dative with Ἀγαμέμνονι.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
πορφύρεον μέγα φᾶρος ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ παχείῃ,
sentences.l:
He went on his way, along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans,
a great purple cloak holding in his stout hand,
sentences.i: He set off along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans, holding a great purple cloak in his stout hand,
sentences.n: The subject is Agamemnon, named in the previous unit. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is ‘he set out to go’ (βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω, ἰέναι the infinitive of εἶμι), and παρά … κλισίας … νῆας is ‘along the huts and the ships’. The cloak is πορφύρεον … φᾶρος, ‘purple cloak’ (πορφύρεος is a dark, gleaming colour), held ἐν χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘in his stout hand’. The text does not say why he carries it.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἐπ’ Ὀδυσσῆος μεγακήτεϊ νηῒ μελαίνῃ,
ἥ ῥ’ ἐν μεσσάτῳ ἔσκε γεγωνέμεν ἀμφοτέρωσε,
sentences.l:
and he stood by Odysseus’ huge black ship,
which was in the middle, to be heard on both sides,
sentences.i: and stood by the huge black ship of Odysseus, which lay in the middle, so that a shout carried in both directions,
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘he stood’, and Ὀδυσσῆος has the double σ of the epic genitive. μεγακήτεϊ, an epithet of ships, is taken as ‘huge’ (μέγα- and κῆτος ‘sea-monster’), but the formation is not secure; νηῒ μελαίνῃ is the ordinary ‘black ship’. ἥ is a relative pronoun and ἔσκε is the iterative past of εἰμί (‘used to be’). γεγωνέμεν is the infinitive of γεγωνέω ‘call out so as to be heard’ in epic -μεν: the ship lay midway, so that a voice from it carried both ways (ἀμφοτέρωσε ‘to both sides’).

sentences.t:
ἠμὲν ἐπ’ Αἴαντος κλισίας Τελαμωνιάδαο
ἠδ’ ἐπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος, τοί ῥ’ ἔσχατα νῆας ἐΐσας
εἴρυσαν, ἠνορέῃ πίσυνοι καὶ κάρτεϊ χειρῶν·
sentences.i: both to the huts of Ajax, son of Telamon, and to those of Achilles, who had drawn up their well-balanced ships at the farthest ends, trusting in their manliness and the strength of their hands;
sentences.n: ἠμέν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’, with ἐπ’ ‘to’ before each name, and the huts of Ajax and of Achilles lie at the two ends of the line of ships, as ἔσχατα ‘farthest’ shows; a shout from the middle ship carries to both. Τελαμωνιάδαο is a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο, ‘son of Telamon’. τοί is the epic relative ‘who’, picking up the two men; εἴρυσαν is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw (a ship) up the beach’, and ἠνορέῃ … κάρτεϊ χειρῶν is ‘in manliness and strength of hands’, the datives going with πίσυνοι ‘trusting in’.

sentences.t: ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Δαναοῖσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.l: And he shouted, piercingly, calling to the Danaans:
sentences.i: and he shouted piercingly, calling out to the Danaans:
sentences.n: ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’, printed with a diaeresis to show that the two vowels are sounded apart; διαπρύσιον is adverbial, ‘piercingly, right through’. γεγωνώς is the perfect participle of the verb seen at 223, ‘calling out so as to be heard’, and Δαναοῖσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Danaans’.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς Ἀργεῖοι, κάκ’ ἐλέγχεα, εἶδος ἀγητοί·
sentences.l: “Shame, Argives, base disgraces, admirable in form!
sentences.i: “Shame, Argives, you base disgraces, admirable in form!
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s shout begins and runs to the end of his prayer at 244. αἰδώς is ‘shame’ as an exclamation, and Ἀργεῖοι is the vocative. κάκ’ ἐλέγχεα is κακὰ ἐλέγχεα ‘base disgraces’, neuter plural and an insult; εἶδος ἀγητοί is ‘admirable in form’, εἶδος being an accusative of respect and ἀγητοί a verbal adjective of ἄγαμαι ‘admire’. The sting is that they look splendid and are not.

sentences.t:
πῇ ἔβαν εὐχωλαί, ὅτε δὴ φάμεν εἶναι ἄριστοι,
ἃς ὁπότ’ ἐν Λήμνῳ κενεαυχέες ἠγοράασθε,
sentences.l:
Where have they gone, the boasts, when indeed we said that we were best,
which, when in Lemnos, empty-boasters, you proclaimed,
sentences.i: Where have the boasts gone, when we said we were the best, the boasts you proclaimed at Lemnos, empty boasters that you were,
sentences.n: The question runs on through the next unit. ἔβαν is an aorist, ‘have gone’ (= ἔβησαν), and εὐχωλαί are ‘boasts’. ὅτε δὴ φάμεν εἶναι ἄριστοι is ‘when we said we were the best’: φάμεν is the first plural of φημί, used for a past boast (the accent marks it as an unaugmented imperfect, not the present), with the speaker including himself. ἃς … ἠγοράασθε takes ἃς ‘which’ as its object, the boasts, and ἠγοράασθε is the second plural imperfect of ἀγοράομαι ‘speak out, proclaim’ (Attic ἠγορᾶσθε), uncontracted. κενεαυχέες, ‘empty-boasting’, is a vocative plural. Lemnos is an island in the northern Aegean.

sentences.t:
ἔσθοντες κρέα πολλὰ βοῶν ὀρθοκραιράων
πίνοντες κρητῆρας ἐπιστεφέας οἴνοιο,
Τρώων ἄνθ’ ἑκατόν τε διηκοσίων τε ἕκαστος
στήσεσθ’ ἐν πολέμῳ·
sentences.l:
eating much flesh of straight-horned cattle
and drinking mixing-bowls brimming with wine,
against a hundred and two hundred of the Trojans, each one of you,
you will stand in war;
sentences.i: eating plenty of the flesh of straight-horned cattle and drinking mixing-bowls brimming with wine, that each of you would stand in battle against a hundred or two hundred Trojans;
sentences.n: ἔσθοντες ‘eating’ (ἔσθω is a by-form of ἐσθίω) and πίνοντες ‘drinking’ belong to the ‘you’ of ἠγοράασθε: the boasts were made at the feast. ὀρθοκραιράων ‘straight-horned’ (ὀρθός ‘straight’ and the root of κέρας ‘horn’) goes with βοῶν ‘cattle’. κρητῆρας ἐπιστεφέας οἴνοιο is ‘mixing-bowls brimming with wine’, the bowls in which wine was mixed with water. Τρώων ἄνθ’ ἑκατόν τε διηκοσίων τε ἕκαστος is ‘against a hundred and two hundred of the Trojans, each one’: ἄνθ’ is ἀντί ‘against, in place of’, and ‘a hundred and two hundred’ means a hundred or two. στήσεσθ’ is the future middle of ἵστημι, ‘you will take your stand’, giving the content of the boast; the English reports it as indirect speech.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οὐδ’ ἑνὸς ἄξιοί εἰμεν
Ἕκτορος, ὃς τάχα νῆας ἐνιπρήσει πυρὶ κηλέῳ.
sentences.l:
But now not even of one are we worthy,
of Hector, who soon the ships will burn with blazing fire.
sentences.i: But now we are not worth even one Hector, who will soon burn the ships with blazing fire.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ sets the present against the boast. ἄξιοί εἰμεν is ‘we are worth’ (εἰμέν is the epic first plural of εἰμί), with a genitive of value, οὐδ’ ἑνὸς … Ἕκτορος ‘not even one … Hector’: all the army together is not worth a single Hector. ὃς τάχα … ἐνιπρήσει is ‘who will soon burn’, ἐνιπρήσει being the future of the verb seen in ἐνέπρησεν earlier. πυρὶ κηλέῳ is ‘with blazing fire’, as before.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἦ ῥά τιν’ ἤδη ὑπερμενέων βασιλήων
τῇδ’ ἄτῃ ἄασας καί μιν μέγα κῦδος ἀπηύρας;
sentences.l:
Father Zeus, have you indeed already any of the exceeding-strong kings
with this bewilderment bewildered, and from him great glory taken away?
sentences.i: Father Zeus, have you ever yet bewildered one of the kings of surpassing strength with a bewilderment like this, and taken great glory from him?
sentences.n: Agamemnon turns from the army to Zeus; the quotation goes on. Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. ἦ ῥά opens a pointed question, ‘can it be that …?’, and ἤδη is ‘already, ever yet’. ὑπερμενέων βασιλήων is ‘of the kings of surpassing strength’, a genitive plural after τιν’ ‘any’. τῇδ’ ἄτῃ ἄασας pairs a verb with its own noun: ἄτη is ‘bewilderment’, the clouding of a man’s mind that leads him to ruin, and ἄασας is the aorist of ἀάω ‘bewilder’. μιν μέγα κῦδος ἀπηύρας is ‘took great glory from him’: ἀπηύρας is an aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, with the person (μιν) and the thing (κῦδος) both in the accusative.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν δή ποτέ φημι τεὸν περικαλλέα βωμὸν
νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι παρελθέμεν ἐνθάδε ἔρρων,
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσι βοῶν δημὸν καὶ μηρί’ ἔκηα
ἱέμενος Τροίην εὐτείχεον ἐξαλαπάξαι.
sentences.l:
Never indeed ever, I say, your very beautiful altar
in a many-thwarted ship to have passed by, coming here wretchedly,
but upon all the fat of oxen and thigh-pieces I burned,
longing well-walled Troy to plunder utterly.
sentences.i: I say that I have never passed your very beautiful altar in a ship of many thwarts on my wretched way here, but upon every one I burned the fat of oxen and thigh-pieces, longing to plunder well-walled Troy.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν δή ποτέ φημι … παρελθέμεν is ‘I say that I never passed’: φημι takes an infinitive, and παρελθέμεν is the aorist infinitive of παρέρχομαι in epic -έμεν (Attic παρελθεῖν). τεὸν … βωμόν ‘your altar’ is its object (τεόν = σόν). νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι is ‘in a ship of many thwarts’, κληΐς being a thwart or rowing-bench, and ἔρρων is ‘going wretchedly’ (ἔρρω ‘go with ill luck’), his hapless way to Troy. ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσι is ‘but upon all’, the noun not given; βοῶν δημόν ‘the fat of oxen’ and μηρία ‘thigh-pieces’ are the parts burned for a god, and ἔκηα is the aorist of καίω. ἱέμενος is ‘longing’ (ἵεμαι), and ἐξαλαπάξαι ‘to plunder utterly’ is an aorist infinitive.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ Ζεῦ τόδε πέρ μοι ἐπικρήηνον ἐέλδωρ·
sentences.l: But, Zeus, this at least for me fulfil, the wish:
sentences.i: But, Zeus, fulfil at least this wish for me:
sentences.n: A short prayer after the complaint. ἀλλά … πέρ is ‘but at least’. ἐπικρήηνον is the aorist imperative of ἐπικραιαίνω ‘bring to fulfilment’ in its epic form, and ἐέλδωρ ‘wish’ stands beside τόδε; the wish itself is given in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτοὺς δή περ ἔασον ὑπεκφυγέειν καὶ ἀλύξαι,
μηδ’ οὕτω Τρώεσσιν ἔα δάμνασθαι Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
Ourselves, at least, allow to flee away and to escape,
and not thus by the Trojans allow to be subdued the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: At least allow us ourselves to flee away and escape, and do not let the Achaeans be subdued by the Trojans like this.”
sentences.n: ἔασον and ἔα are the aorist and present imperatives of ἐάω ‘allow, let’. The first takes αὐτούς ‘ourselves’ as the subject of the infinitives ὑπεκφυγέειν ‘flee away’ (epic -έειν, Attic ὑπεκφυγεῖν) and ἀλύξαι ‘escape’. μηδ’ οὕτω … ἔα … δάμνασθαι is the negative request: δάμνασθαι is the passive infinitive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, with the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘by the Trojans’ in epic -εσσι. The prayer, and Agamemnon’s speech, end here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τὸν δὲ πατὴρ ὀλοφύρατο δάκρυ χέοντα,
νεῦσε δέ οἱ λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι οὐδ’ ἀπολέσθαι.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and him the father grieved for, a tear shedding,
and nodded to him that the people be safe and not perish.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Father grieved for him as he shed tears, and nodded to him that the people should be safe and not perish.
sentences.n: πατήρ ‘the father’ is Zeus, not named. ὣς φάτο is the stock closing of a speech (φάτο = ἔφατο without the augment). ὀλοφύρατο is the aorist of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘grieve for’, the verb Hera used at 8.202 of Poseidon’s heart, and δάκρυ χέοντα, ‘shedding a tear’, agrees with τόν (Agamemnon). νεῦσε ‘nodded’ is the gesture of assent, and what is granted is put in an accusative and infinitive, λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι οὐδ’ ἀπολέσθαι ‘that the people be safe and not perish’ (σόον is the older form of σῶν ‘safe’, ἔμμεναι = εἶναι). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ αἰετὸν ἧκε τελειότατον πετεηνῶν,
νεβρὸν ἔχοντ’ ὀνύχεσσι τέκος ἐλάφοιο ταχείης·
sentences.l:
At once an eagle he sent, the most perfect of winged things,
a fawn holding in its talons, the young of a swift deer;
sentences.i: At once he sent an eagle, the most perfect of winged creatures, holding in its talons a fawn, the young of a swift deer;
sentences.n: An omen. αἰετόν ‘eagle’ is the object of ἧκε (the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’), and Zeus is the sender, as the later words ἐκ Διός show. τελειότατον is the superlative of τέλειος ‘perfect, complete’; the usual explanation is that this is the eagle whose sign is surest to be fulfilled, and πετεηνῶν is the genitive plural ‘of winged creatures’. νεβρὸν ἔχοντ’ ὀνύχεσσι is ‘holding a fawn in its talons’ (ἔχοντ’ is the accusative participle with its last vowel cut off, ὀνύχεσσι the epic dative plural), and τέκος ἐλάφοιο ταχείης ‘the young of a swift deer’ explains νεβρόν.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δὲ Διὸς βωμῷ περικαλλέϊ κάββαλε νεβρόν,
ἔνθα πανομφαίῳ Ζηνὶ ῥέζεσκον Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
and beside the altar of Zeus, the very beautiful, it dropped the fawn,
where to Zeus of every divine voice used to sacrifice the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and beside the very beautiful altar of Zeus it dropped the fawn, where the Achaeans used to sacrifice to Zeus, the source of every divine voice.
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά ‘beside’, and Διὸς βωμῷ περικαλλέϊ is ‘the very beautiful altar of Zeus’; κάββαλε is κατέβαλε shortened and assimilated, ‘threw down, dropped’. ἔνθα … ῥέζεσκον says that the Achaeans ‘used to sacrifice’ there, ῥέζεσκον being an iterative imperfect (epic -σκ-). πανομφαίῳ is a rare epithet of Zeus built on πᾶν ‘all’ and ὀμφή ‘voice of a god’, so ‘from whom every divine voice comes’; that is the usual explanation, and the exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὡς οὖν εἴδονθ’ ὅ τ’ ἄρ’ ἐκ Διὸς ἤλυθεν ὄρνις,
μᾶλλον ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι θόρον, μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.l:
And they, when then they saw that from Zeus had come the bird,
the more upon the Trojans leapt, and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.i: And when they saw that the bird had come from Zeus, they leapt the more upon the Trojans and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ are the Achaeans. εἴδονθ’ is εἴδοντο, a middle aorist of ‘see’ with its last vowel cut off (the τ shows as θ before the rough breathing of ὅ); ὅ is the conjunction ‘that’, followed by τε and ἄρα. The bird has come ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’, and the Achaeans take it as his answer. θόρον is the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’ without the augment, and μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης is ‘they remembered the joy of battle’, μιμνῄσκομαι taking the genitive; χάρμη is the joy and eagerness of fighting.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔ τις πρότερος Δαναῶν πολλῶν περ ἐόντων
εὔξατο Τυδεΐδαο πάρος σχέμεν ὠκέας ἵππους
τάφρου τ’ ἐξελάσαι καὶ ἐναντίβιον μαχέσασθαι,
sentences.l:
Then none earlier of the Danaans, many though being,
claimed before the son of Tydeus to hold the swift horses
and to drive out of the ditch and to fight head-on,
sentences.i: Then no one of the Danaans, many though they were, could claim to have been earlier than the son of Tydeus in reining in his swift horses, driving out of the ditch, and fighting head-on,
sentences.n: The son of Tydeus is Diomedes: Τυδεΐδαο is the epic genitive of Τυδεΐδης. οὔ τις πρότερος … Τυδεΐδαο πάρος is ‘no one earlier than the son of Tydeus’ (πρότερος and πάρος both mean ‘before’, and the genitive is one of comparison). εὔξατο is the aorist of εὔχομαι, here ‘claimed’, not ‘prayed’, and it governs the three infinitives. σχέμεν is the aorist infinitive of ἔχω ‘hold’ in epic -μεν, with ὠκέας ἵππους ‘swift horses’; the sense, checking or steering the team, is the usual reading. τάφρου ἐξελάσαι is ‘drive out of the ditch’ (the genitive of separation, ἐξελάσαι an aorist infinitive of ἐξελαύνω), and ἐναντίβιον μαχέσασθαι is ‘to fight head-on’, literally ‘against his strength’. Δαναῶν πολλῶν περ ἐόντων is ‘of the Danaans, many though they were’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρῶτος Τρώων ἕλεν ἄνδρα κορυστὴν
Φραδμονίδην Ἀγέλαον·
sentences.l:
but by far the first of the Trojans he took a helmeted man,
Phradmon’s-son Agelaus;
sentences.i: but he by far was the first to kill a helmeted warrior of the Trojans, Agelaus, son of Phradmon;
sentences.n: The subject, still unnamed, is Diomedes. πολὺ πρῶτος is ‘by far the first’, and Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’ is taken with ἄνδρα. ἕλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, here ‘kill’, and ἄνδρα κορυστήν is ‘a helmeted warrior’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’). Φραδμονίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Phradmon’, in the accusative beside Ἀγέλαον.

sentences.t: ὃ μὲν φύγαδ’ ἔτραπεν ἵππους·
sentences.l: he, on the one hand, to flight turned his horses;
sentences.i: he turned his horses to flight;
sentences.n: ὃ μέν ‘he, on the one hand’ is Agelaus, and the μέν is balanced by the δέ of the next unit, where Diomedes strikes him. φύγαδε is ‘to flight’, the suffix -δε giving the direction and the final vowel cut off, and ἔτραπεν is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ μεταστρεφθέντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πῆξεν
ὤμων μεσσηγύς, διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσεν·
sentences.l:
and to him, as he turned about, in the back the spear he fixed,
between the shoulders, and through the chest he drove it;
sentences.i: and as he turned about, he fixed his spear in his back, between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘him’ is Agelaus, and μεταστρεφθέντι is the aorist passive participle of μεταστρέφω, ‘having been turned about’, in the dative with it. μεταφρένῳ is the dative of μετάφρενον ‘the back’, the place hit; ἐν … πῆξεν is ‘fixed in’, the preposition standing apart from the verb (tmesis), and δόρυ ‘spear’ is the object. ὤμων μεσσηγύς is ‘between the shoulders’, and διὰ … ἔλασσεν is ‘drove through’, again in tmesis, with στήθεσφιν, the dative in -φιν, ‘through the chest’. The subject is still Diomedes.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l: He crashed down from the chariot, and clattered, upon him, his armour.
sentences.i: He crashed down from his chariot, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: Agelaus falls. ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’, and ὀχέων is the plural of ὄχος, ‘chariot’. ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ is a verb that imitates the sound, used here of armour striking as a man falls; τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is ‘upon him’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μετ’ Ἀτρεΐδαι Ἀγαμέμνων καὶ Μενέλαος,
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Αἴαντες θοῦριν ἐπιειμένοι ἀλκήν,
sentences.l:
And after him the Atreus’-sons, Agamemnon and Menelaus,
and after them the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might,
sentences.i: After him came the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, and after them the two Ajaxes, clothed in impetuous might,
sentences.n: A list of those who come after Diomedes. It has no verb; ‘came’ is supplied from μετά and ἐπί. τόν is Diomedes, μετ’ is μετά ‘after’, and Ἀτρεΐδαι is the epic nominative plural, ‘sons of Atreus’, here Agamemnon and Menelaus. τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ ‘and after them’ (ἐπί with the dative of the group just named) begins each step of the list. Αἴαντες ‘the two Ajaxes’ is the plural for the pair of that name, the son of Telamon and the son of Oileus. θοῦριν ἐπιειμένοι ἀλκήν is ‘clothed in impetuous might’, the participle being the perfect middle of ἕννυμι. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Ἰδομενεὺς καὶ ὀπάων Ἰδομενῆος
Μηριόνης ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ,
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.i: and after them Idomeneus and Idomeneus’ follower Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men, and after them Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son;
sentences.n: The list goes on without a verb. ὀπάων ‘follower’ is what Meriones is to Idomeneus, and Μηριόνης stands beside it; Ἰδομενῆος is the genitive of Ἰδομενεύς with the Ionic ending -ῆος. ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ is ‘the equal of Enyalius, killer of men’, Enyalius being a name of the war-god, and ἀνδρειφόντῃ a dative built on ἀνήρ ‘man’ and the root of φόνος ‘killing’. Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός is ‘Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son’. Line 264 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and Ἐνυαλίῳ has to be scanned with synizesis, the -ιῳ as one syllable. Line 265 is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the third foot the short final syllable of Εὐρύπυλος has to be taken as long before the vowel of Εὐαίμονος.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρος δ’ εἴνατος ἦλθε παλίντονα τόξα τιταίνων,
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ Αἴαντος σάκεϊ Τελαμωνιάδαο.
sentences.l:
And Teucer, ninth, came, the back-stretched bow stretching,
and stood then under the shield of Ajax, Telamon’s-son.
sentences.i: Teucer came ninth, stretching his recurved bow, and stood beneath the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon.
sentences.n: Teucer is ninth in the count: Diomedes, the two sons of Atreus, the two Ajaxes, Idomeneus, Meriones and Eurypylus come before him. εἴνατος is the Ionic ordinal ‘ninth’ (Attic ἔνατος). παλίντονα τόξα is ‘recurved bow’, from πάλιν ‘back’ and τείνω ‘stretch’; τόξα is plural in form, and the exact shape of the bow is not known. τιταίνων ‘stretching’ is the participle of τιταίνω (= τείνω). στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ … σάκεϊ is ‘and stood under the shield’ (σάκεϊ the epic dative of σάκος), with Αἴαντος … Τελαμωνιάδαο ‘of Ajax, son of Telamon’; Teucer’s own father is named at 283 as Telamon too.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Αἴας μὲν ὑπεξέφερεν σάκος·
sentences.l: Then Ajax, on the one hand, would draw his shield aside;
sentences.i: Then Ajax would draw his shield aside;
sentences.n: From here to 272 the verbs are iterative and the picture is of a routine repeated again and again. ὑπεξέφερεν is the imperfect of ὑπεκφέρω, ‘carry out from under’: Ajax moves his shield away so that Teucer can look out and shoot. μὲν … αὐτάρ sets Ajax against Teucer, who is the subject of the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
παπτήνας, ἐπεὶ ἄρ τιν’ ὀϊστεύσας ἐν ὁμίλῳ
βεβλήκοι, ὃ μὲν αὖθι πεσὼν ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσεν,
sentences.l:
but he, the hero,
having glanced around, when someone he had shot with an arrow in the throng
and hit, that man, falling right there, lost his life,
sentences.i: and the hero, glancing about, whenever he had shot an arrow at someone in the throng and hit him, that man would fall on the spot and lose his life,
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ ἥρως is Teucer, ‘the hero’ (ἥρως is a word for a warrior). παπτήνας is the aorist participle of παπταίνω ‘glance about’. ἐπεὶ … βεβλήκοι is an iterative clause in past time, the optative of the perfect, ‘whenever he had hit’, with ὀϊστεύσας ‘having shot an arrow’ (from ὀϊστός ‘arrow’) and ἐν ὁμίλῳ ‘in the throng’. ὃ μέν ‘that man’ is the one hit, who πεσὼν αὖθι, ‘falling right there’, ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὄλεσσεν ‘lost his life’: ἀπό is separated from the verb (tmesis), and ὄλεσσεν has the epic -σσ-.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ αὖτις ἰὼν πάϊς ὣς ὑπὸ μητέρα δύσκεν
εἰς Αἴανθ’·
sentences.l:
but he, going back again, like a child, under his mother
would slip in, to Ajax;
sentences.i: but he would go back again, like a child to its mother, and slip in beside Ajax;
sentences.n: δύσκεν is the iterative imperfect of δύω ‘go in, slip under’ (epic -σκ-, without the augment). ὑπὸ μητέρα … εἰς Αἴανθ’ runs the comparison and what it compares together: ‘like a child under its mother, (he would go) to Ajax’. ἰών is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’, αὖτις is ‘again’, and πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς ‘child’. Αἴανθ’ is Αἴαντα, the accusative of Αἴας.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ μιν σάκεϊ κρύπτασκε φαεινῷ.
sentences.l: and he would hide him with his shield, gleaming.
sentences.i: and Ajax would hide him with his gleaming shield.
sentences.n: κρύπτασκε is the iterative imperfect of κρύπτω ‘hide’ (epic -σκ-). ὃ δέ is Ajax and μιν is Teucer; σάκεϊ … φαεινῷ is ‘with his gleaming shield’, φαεινῷ agreeing with σάκεϊ.

sentences.t: ἔνθα τίνα πρῶτον Τρώων ἕλε Τεῦκρος ἀμύμων;
sentences.l: Then whom first of the Trojans did Teucer take, the blameless?
sentences.i: Then whom did blameless Teucer kill first of the Trojans?
sentences.n: The poet puts a question to himself, and the list that follows is the answer. ἔνθα is ‘then, there’, τίνα ‘whom’, and ἕλε the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took, killed’. ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet, translated every time in the same way. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ὀρσίλοχον μὲν πρῶτα καὶ Ὄρμενον ἠδ’ Ὀφελέστην
Δαίτορά τε Χρομίον τε καὶ ἀντίθεον Λυκοφόντην
καὶ Πολυαιμονίδην Ἀμοπάονα καὶ Μελάνιππον,
πάντας ἐπασσυτέρους πέλασε χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ.
sentences.l:
Orsilochus first, and Ormenus, and Ophelestes,
and Daetor and Chromius and godlike Lycophontes,
and Amopaon, Polyaemon’s-son, and Melanippus,
all one close upon another he brought to the much-nourishing earth.
sentences.i: He killed Orsilochus first, then Ormenus and Ophelestes, Daetor and Chromius and godlike Lycophontes, and Amopaon, son of Polyaemon, and Melanippus, bringing them all down one after another to the earth that feeds so many.
sentences.n: The answer is a list of eight names, all in the accusative as objects of πέλασε, the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, which here carries the sense of bringing them down to the earth. πάντας ἐπασσυτέρους is ‘all of them in quick succession’. Πολυαιμονίδην Ἀμοπάονα is ‘Amopaon, son of Polyaemon’, with a patronymic in apposition, and ἀντίθεον ‘godlike’ is the stock epithet. χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ is ‘to the much-nourishing earth’, πουλυβοτείρῃ being the epic form of πολυβότειρα with a lengthened first syllable.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ἰδὼν γήθησεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
τόξου ἄπο κρατεροῦ Τρώων ὀλέκοντα φάλαγγας·
sentences.l:
And him, seeing, rejoiced lord of men Agamemnon,
from the strong bow the Trojan battle-lines destroying;
sentences.i: And lord of men Agamemnon rejoiced when he saw him destroying the Trojan battle-lines with his strong bow;
sentences.n: τόν is Teucer, the object of ἰδών ‘seeing’. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is the stock ‘lord of men’. τόξου ἄπο κρατεροῦ is ‘from (with) the strong bow’, ἄπο standing after its noun with its accent drawn back. ὀλέκοντα is the participle of ὀλέκω ‘destroy’, agreeing with τόν, and φάλαγγας are the ‘battle-lines’ of the Trojans.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ παρ’ αὐτὸν ἰὼν καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: and he stood beside him, going up, and addressed him with a word:
sentences.i: He went up and stood beside him and spoke to him:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘he stood’, παρ’ αὐτόν ‘beside him’, and ἰών ‘going’, so he went up and stood by Teucer. καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε is ‘and addressed him with a word’, πρὸς … ἔειπε being πρός separated from the verb (tmesis).

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρε φίλη κεφαλή, Τελαμώνιε κοίρανε λαῶν
βάλλ’ οὕτως, αἴ κέν τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένηαι
πατρί τε σῷ Τελαμῶνι, ὅ σ’ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα,
καί σε νόθον περ ἐόντα κομίσσατο ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ·
sentences.l:
“Teucer, dear head, son of Telamon, ruler of the people,
shoot thus, if somehow a light you may become to the Danaans
and to your father Telamon, who reared you when little,
and you, illegitimate though being, took care of in his own house;
sentences.i: “Teucer, dear head, son of Telamon, ruler of the people, shoot on like this, in the hope that you may somehow become a light to the Danaans and to your father Telamon, who reared you when you were small and, illegitimate though you were, took care of you in his own house;
sentences.n: Teucer is addressed in the vocative. φίλη κεφαλή, ‘dear head’, is an affectionate address, the head standing for the man; Τελαμώνιε is the adjective ‘Telamonian, son of Telamon’, and κοίρανε λαῶν is ‘ruler of the people’. βάλλ’ is the present imperative of βάλλω, ‘keep shooting’. αἴ κέν τι … γένηαι is ‘in case you may somehow become’ (αἴ = εἰ, and γένηαι the epic -ηαι subjunctive of γίγνομαι); φόως ‘light’ is a figure for rescue and relief. ὅ σ’ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα is ‘who reared you when you were small’, and νόθον περ ἐόντα ‘illegitimate though you were’ is what makes the care remarkable. κομίσσατο is the aorist middle of κομίζω ‘take care of’, with the epic -σσ-, and ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ‘in his own house’. Agamemnon’s speech to Teucer begins here.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ τηλόθ’ ἐόντα ἐϋκλείης ἐπίβησον.
sentences.l: Him, even far away being, upon good fame cause to step.
sentences.i: Bring him, too, far away though he is, to good fame.
sentences.n: τόν is Telamon, who is not at Troy: τηλόθ’ is τηλόθι ‘far off’, with τὸν καὶ … ἐόντα ‘him even though he is’. ἐπίβησον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιβαίνω in its causative sense, ‘make to stand upon’, and it takes the genitive ἐϋκλείης ‘good fame’ (εὐκλείη, in the Ionic form with ἐϋ-). The thought is that the father shares in his son’s glory.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐγὼ ἐξερέω ὡς καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.l: And to you I will tell out how it also will be accomplished:
sentences.i: And I will tell you how it will really be accomplished:
sentences.n: Agamemnon moves from encouragement to promise. ἐξερέω is the future of ἐξερέω ‘speak out, declare’ (epic uncontracted -έω), and ὡς … ἔσται is an indirect question, ‘how it will be’. τετελεσμένον ἔσται is a periphrastic future, the perfect participle of τελέω ‘accomplish’ with ἔσται, ‘will have been accomplished’, and καί here is ‘really, indeed’. The promise follows in the next two units.

sentences.t:
αἴ κέν μοι δώῃ Ζεύς τ’ αἰγίοχος καὶ Ἀθήνη
Ἰλίου ἐξαλαπάξαι ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
sentences.l:
If to me should give Zeus, aegis-bearing, and Athena
to plunder utterly the well-built citadel of Ilium,
sentences.i: if aegis-bearing Zeus and Athena grant me to plunder the well-built citadel of Ilium,
sentences.n: αἴ κέν μοι δώῃ is ‘if ever … should grant me’ (αἴ = εἰ; δώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι, in the epic form for Attic δῷ), and the verb is singular although there are two subjects. Ζεύς τ’ αἰγίοχος is ‘aegis-bearing Zeus’; the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed, and ‘holding the aegis’ is the usual explanation. ἐξαλαπάξαι is ‘to plunder utterly’, ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον ‘the well-built citadel’, and Ἰλίου ‘of Ilium’, that is Troy. The result of the condition is the promise in the next unit.

sentences.t:
πρώτῳ τοι μετ’ ἐμὲ πρεσβήϊον ἐν χερὶ θήσω,
ἢ τρίποδ’ ἠὲ δύω ἵππους αὐτοῖσιν ὄχεσφιν
ἠὲ γυναῖχ’, ἥ κέν τοι ὁμὸν λέχος εἰσαναβαίνοι.
sentences.l:
to you first, after me, a prize of precedence into your hand I will put,
either a tripod, or two horses, with the very chariot,
or a woman, who might go up into the same bed with you.”
sentences.i: I will put a prize of honour in your hand, to you first after myself: either a tripod, or two horses with the chariot itself, or a woman, one who would go up into the same bed with you.”
sentences.n: πρώτῳ τοι μετ’ ἐμέ is ‘to you first after me’ (τοι = σοι). πρεσβήϊον is a prize of honour, a rare word built on πρέσβυς ‘elder’, the honour due to rank, and Agamemnon will put it ἐν χερὶ θήσω ‘in your hand’. Three choices follow, joined by ἢ … ἠέ … ἠέ ‘either … or … or’: a τρίπους (here a tripod), δύω ἵππους αὐτοῖσιν ὄχεσφιν ‘two horses with the chariot itself’ (δύω is the epic form of δύο, and ὄχεσφιν a dative in -φιν), and a woman ἥ κέν τοι ὁμὸν λέχος εἰσαναβαίνοι ‘who would go up into the same bed with you’, the optative with κε saying what the prize is for. Women are among the prizes given to a warrior. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.
